solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: (& 4ac.) The opposition he'll have soundly beaten to stay at the top

definitions.text: The opposition he'll have soundly beaten to stay at the top

parts.words: The opposition he'll have soundly beaten
parts.note: surface reading: a leader who trounces his rivals at the polls
setter's reading: a strongman whose opponents are robbed and mugged, the words 'soundly' hints are heard in his name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Soundly beaten' looks like 'decisively defeated', but 'soundly' also points to sound: say the name and you hear 'robber, mugger'. The Zimbabwean president clung to power by intimidating the opposition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Zimbabwean leader kept power for decades through rigged votes and violence against opposition supporters, so the clue is a portrait of him.

clue.text: Arse let out to cover tip of trouser snake

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap round it, so the shuffled letters sit either side of the trouser tip
letting the letters go frees them from their places, so they fall into a new order
out means gone, so one letter of the little word leaves it, the vowel

parts.note: the rear is the backside
taken as written

indicators.note: 'tip of' keeps only the first letter of 'trouser'

parts.note: the tip of trouser is its first letter

explanation.surface: A crude image of a bodily emission threatening a man's trousers and their contents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouser snake' reads as slang for the penis, but the definition is just 'snake'. The wordplay is loose: the vowel of the little word has to go before the mix, and 'let' works twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A rattler is the informal name for a rattlesnake, the venomous American serpent with a noisy tail.

clue.text: Brenda's own bit of rough at breakfast? "One's captivated"

indicators.note: something captivated is held captive, so the word for one is held inside the breakfast food

parts.note: bran is roughage eaten at breakfast
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A cheeky suggestion that the Queen keeps a rough lover at the breakfast table.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls the Queen 'Brenda', so 'Brenda's own' is Queen's own: Brian May, the band Queen's guitarist. 'Bit of rough' is a lower-class lover, but here it is cereal roughage.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian May is the guitarist of the rock band Queen, so he belongs to Queen as Brenda's own.

clue.text: Hurley with kit off, left for one minister

indicators.note: off here means out of kilter, so the letters are disarranged before they settle
putting one thing for another means swapping it in, so the left letter replaces the one letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Elizabeth Hurley stripping off, cast as some sort of minister.
explanation.walkthrough: In KIT the I is swapped for L, then HURLEY and KLT are rearranged. The surface invites thinking of the actress Liz Hurley undressing.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruth Kelly was a Labour cabinet minister under Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, holding education and transport posts.

clue.text: see 1ac.
Cyclops's organ and balls

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the setter Cyclops has a single eye

explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ and balls' pushes towards anatomy below the belt, but the organ is the setter's one eye and balls means rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical Cyclops had one eye, so the setter speaking of it says 'my eye'; 'my eye!' is also an old exclamation dismissing nonsense.

clue.text: Bog makes soft soldiers

parts.note: soft and gentle are synonyms
soldiers are men in the ranks

explanation.surface: A swamp turning troops soft, or a toilet doing the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bog' is British slang for a toilet, and the sign on a men's public toilet reads 'Gentlemen'.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage 'the gentlemen' or 'the gents' is the men's public toilet, and 'bog' is slang for a toilet.

clue.text: Noble, neat Boris is out rocking

indicators.note: rocking shakes things about, so the remaining letters are jumbled
the two letters of the little word is are declared out, so they leave the name

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson, tidy for once, out somewhere enjoying himself, presented as a nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is out' removes IS from BORIS, leaving BOR to be mixed with NEAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A baronet holds a hereditary British title ranking just below a baron, so is a member of the titled nobility in loose usage.

clue.text: Twit (London's leader) entertained by diplomat — "pain in the arse!"

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is taken in, so these letters go inside the diplomat

parts.note: HE, His Excellency, is the title of an ambassador
an ass is a fool
London's leader is its first letter

explanation.surface: An idiot London mayor being hosted by an ambassador and proving a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: HE stands for His or Her Excellency, the style given to ambassadors; ASS plus L sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hassle is a nuisance or annoying bother, which is what the coarse phrase 'pain in the arse' describes.

clue.text: "Band takes drink with speed and ecstasy starters" provocative revelation

parts.note: a strip is a band of material
tea is a drink

indicators.note: starters are the opening items, so only the first letter of each word counts

parts.note: first letter of speed
first letter of ecstasy

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline about a rock band taking drink and drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted line reads like a scandal story about a pop group; the band is a strip of cloth, and speed and ecstasy give only their initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A striptease is an erotic performance in which clothes are removed gradually, literally revealing the body to tantalise an audience.

clue.text: Labour finally gets in new reviled leader

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so that letter goes inside the word for new

parts.note: neo- is the prefix meaning new; the letter goes between its N-E and O

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word, its last letter

parts.note: the final letter of Labour
the end of NEO, the combining form for new

explanation.surface: A political sketch of a hated party leader coming in at the end of Labour's run.
explanation.walkthrough: NEO is the prefix meaning new, as in neoliberal; R goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nero was the Roman emperor remembered for cruelty and for supposedly fiddling while Rome burned, a byword for a despised ruler.

clue.text: Physicist's method with emptied penis

indicators.note: something emptied has its contents removed, so only the outside letters of the word remain

parts.note: a plan is a method of doing something
cock is slang for penis

explanation.surface: A crude jibe about a scientist's technique involving an exhausted member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Physicist's' reads as possessive, but the 's is 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Planck was the German physicist who founded quantum theory, giving his name to Planck's constant.

clue.text: Entertained by rock star, Brenda's given "line" — "Top-notch!"

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is taken in, so these letters sit inside the rock star

parts.note: Sting, the former Police frontman, opens round the inserted letters
Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda, and ER is the Queen's royal cipher
L is the abbreviation for line
the rest of Sting

explanation.surface: The Queen hosted by a rock star and handed a line of something, which she rates highly.
explanation.walkthrough: The rock star is Sting; 'line' in quotes invites a line of cocaine, but it is just L.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterling as an adjective means of excellent quality, from the high silver standard of British currency.

clue.text: Right depressed being a confirmed Cameron supporter?

parts.note: right and true are synonyms, as in a true answer
feeling blue is feeling down

explanation.surface: A gloomy right-winger who sticks with David Cameron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' looks political, matching Cameron, but it only means correct. Blue is the British Conservative Party's colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A true blue is a staunch loyal Conservative, blue being the Tory party colour and Cameron its leader.

clue.text: English "hump me" is rewritten as e.g. "Let's play bury the sausage"

indicators.note: something rewritten has been put into different words and order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
these eight letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A crude proposition being rephrased politely as a coy invitation to have sex.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by example: the jokey phrase is itself a coy way of saying something cruder.
explanation.definitionFit: A euphemism is a mild substitute for a blunt word, and 'bury the sausage' is a comic stand-in for sex.

clue.text: see 23ac.
Evades responsibility, heaves up over Victoria's top — infra dig

indicators.note: over here means covering on all sides, so the outer verb is wrapped round the initial
the top of a word is its first letter, so only that letter is taken in

parts.note: to sky a ball is to hit it high into the air, so it skies when heaved up
the first letter of Victoria
behaviour that is a bit off is beneath one, which is what infra dig means

explanation.surface: Someone vomiting over Queen Victoria's head, an undignified scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heaves up' suggests being sick, but it means sending something skywards. Infra dig, short for Latin infra dignitatem, means beneath one's dignity.
explanation.definitionFit: To skive off is British slang for dodging work or duty, which is evading what one is responsible for.

clue.text: Queen-like, Camilla's opening in a big way

indicators.note: an opening is the very start, so only the initial letter of the name is used

parts.note: the first letter of Camilla
amply means abundantly or on a large scale

explanation.surface: Camilla, Prince Charles's wife, making a grand regal entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen-like' suggests royalty next to Camilla, but a queen here is slang for a flamboyant gay man.
explanation.definitionFit: Camp means theatrically effeminate, and queen is slang for an effeminate gay man, so acting like one is acting camply.

clue.text: Party leader extremely lacking meeting Brenda's old social worker

indicators.note: lacking the extremes means the outermost letters at each end are missing

parts.note: Alex Salmond led the Scottish National Party
Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda, and ER is the Queen's royal cipher

explanation.surface: A party leader, lacking much, meeting the Queen's former welfare officer.
explanation.walkthrough: The party leader is Alex Salmond of the Scottish National Party, minus his first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An almoner was formerly a hospital social worker who looked after patients' welfare, a post since renamed.

clue.text: Instrument altering nuts

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters of the word before it go haywire

parts.note: these eight letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tool for adjusting fastenings on a bolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instrument altering nuts' reads as a spanner, but the instrument is musical.
explanation.definitionFit: The triangle is a percussion instrument, a bent steel bar struck with a beater.

clue.text: Stuff getting into tax covenant!

indicators.note: getting into means entering, so the first word goes inside the second

parts.note: to tax someone's patience is to try it; the stuffing goes between its TR and Y
to stuff yourself is to eat greedily
the end of TRY

explanation.surface: Indignation at money being taken under a binding agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax' looks financial, but it means strain or try, as in taxing someone's patience.
explanation.definitionFit: A treaty is a formal agreement between states, and a covenant is likewise a solemn binding agreement.

clue.text: Lousy types stuck outside enclosure leave

indicators.note: being stuck outside something means surrounding it, so these creatures wrap round the abbreviation

parts.note: lice are what make one lousy; the abbreviation goes between LIC and E
enc. is the standard abbreviation for enclosure, as at the foot of a letter
the end of LICE

explanation.surface: Unpleasant people locked out of a compound, told to go away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lousy types' looks like rotten people, but it is literal: lice are the parasites that make you lousy.
explanation.definitionFit: Leave means permission, as in 'by your leave', and a licence is formal permission to do something.

clue.text: Nick Brown's first to enter melée (broadcast) — sounds of sleep to be stifled

indicators.note: to enter means to go inside, so the initial goes into the jumbled letters
something stifled is smothered and held in, so the sleeping sounds are enclosed too
broadcast seed is scattered widely, so these letters land in a new order

parts.note: the five letters rearranged

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of the surname alone

parts.note: the first letter of Brown
zz is the cartoon sound of snoring

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown wading into a televised political scrum while voters doze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' sounds like a man's name beside Brown (Nick Brown was a Labour minister), but it is the verb meaning to steal.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick is British slang for to steal, and to embezzle is to steal money entrusted to one's care.

clue.text: African provides half of Australia with electronic underwear

parts.note: Oz is the nickname for Australia, and half of that two-letter name is its second letter
E is the abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail
a bra is a piece of underwear

explanation.surface: An African trader supplying half of Australia with high-tech undies.
explanation.walkthrough: Oz is the common nickname for Australia, and half of OZ leaves Z. The definition is an animal, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The zebra is a striped wild horse native to Africa, so it is an African animal.

clue.text: Labour not necessarily a welcome prospect for those who do

definitions.text: Labour not necessarily a welcome prospect for those who do

parts.words: Labour not necessarily a welcome prospect
parts.note: surface reading: a Labour government is not something everyone looks forward to
setter's reading: childbirth is a daunting prospect for pregnant women

explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' with its capital looks like the political party, but it is childbirth; pregnant women 'are expecting', so 'those who do' are those who expect.
explanation.definitionFit: To be expecting is the standard euphemism for pregnancy, and labour is what a pregnant woman faces at the end of it.

clue.text: Smashing plus, erection's first beat

indicators.note: smashing something breaks it into pieces that can be reassembled differently

parts.note: the four letters rearranged

indicators.note: first picks out the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the first letter of erection

explanation.surface: A delighted remark that an erection is a great bonus, the first heartbeat of arousal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashing' reads as British slang for excellent, but it signals breaking the letters up.
explanation.definitionFit: A pulse is the regular beat of the heart felt in the arteries, so beat is a direct synonym.

clue.text: (& 14ac.) Nazi type article: it's backed by regressive newspaper editor's leader

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: something backed has been sent backwards, so the little word reads in reverse

parts.note: the word it, with 's standing for is

indicators.note: regressive means going backwards, so the paper's name is read in reverse

parts.note: The Times, the London daily

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the one at the front, its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of editor

explanation.surface: A Nazi writing for a backward right-wing paper under its editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regressive' looks like a political jibe at the paper, but it reverses The Times. The 's of 'it's' is 'is', not part of the reversed word.
explanation.definitionFit: An anti-Semite is someone hostile to Jews, and the Nazis made such hatred their central ideology.

clue.text: Underlying reality of arse having a row

parts.note: bottom is a polite word for backside
a line is a row of things

explanation.surface: A crude pun: the truth beneath it all is a backside getting into an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having a row' suggests a quarrel, but row means a line of things.
explanation.definitionFit: The bottom line is the fundamental truth of a matter, from the final figure in an accounts ledger.

clue.text: Sing out "Mia" vociferously — it's a war scene

indicators.note: vociferously means loudly with the voice, so the words are judged by how they are heard

parts.note: to sing out is to cry out
the name as heard

explanation.surface: Someone loudly calling out a woman's name in some dramatic setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'cry Mia' matches the peninsula's name; Mia sounds like a person to be shouted for.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crimea, on the Black Sea, was the site of the Crimean War of the 1850s, and of later conflicts.

clue.text: Poncey fundraiser's after two large bra sizes

indicators.note: after says which piece comes second, so the fair follows the cup sizes in the answer

parts.note: E and F are large bra cup sizes
a fete is an outdoor fundraising fair; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A charity event's organiser chasing a buxom pair, a camp kind of farce.
explanation.walkthrough: A fete is a British village fair held to raise money. 'Fundraiser's after' means FETE comes after the cup sizes.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete means weak and affected or over-refined, and poncey is British slang for the same pretentious effeminacy.
